clue.text: Island hunter's pessimistic expectation

definitions.meaning: the Caribbean island paired with Trinidad
a gloomy hunter expects to bag nothing at all, with the letter O standing for nothing or zero

explanation.surface: A hunter on an island braces for a disappointing day's shooting.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is a whimsical one: split the answer as TO BAG O, what a hunter who expects to catch nothing would say.
explanation.definitionFit: Tobago is the smaller of the two main islands of the Caribbean state Trinidad and Tobago.

clue.text: Dealer and swindler accepting a couple of fines

indicators.note: the swindler accepts, taking the other letters into the middle of itself

parts.note: a tricker is someone who tricks or cons people
F is the abbreviation for fine, as on pencil leads, so two of them make FF

explanation.surface: A drug dealer who is also a con artist pays a pair of fines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fines' looks like penalties; it is the pencil-grade abbreviation. 'And' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A trafficker deals in illegal goods such as drugs, so is an illicit dealer.

clue.text: Train runners once to take in gas up pipe

indicators.note: the old railway's letters take in the other piece, holding it between them

parts.note: BR is British Rail, which ran the trains in Britain until privatisation

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word is read from bottom to top, so backwards

parts.note: air is a mixture of gases

explanation.surface: Old railway staff once pumped gas up a pipeline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up' turns AIR into RIA, which BR takes in. 'Pipe' is a tobacco pipe made of briar root.
explanation.definitionFit: A briar is a tobacco pipe carved from the root of the briar heath.

clue.text: Elderly lady with a recently emptied breadbasket

parts.note: gran is short for grandmother, an elderly lady

indicators.note: emptied means the inside is removed, leaving only the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: An old woman has just cleared out her bread container.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Emptied' leaves R and Y, the outer letters of 'recently'. 'With' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A granary is a grain store, and a breadbasket figuratively means a grain-producing region or store.

clue.text: Raise protest vocally at time that soldier used to march?

parts.note: to jack, as in jack up a car, is to raise it
to boo is to jeer out loud in protest

explanation.surface: A crowd jeers at the hour a soldier set off marching.
explanation.definitionFit: A jackboot is the tall military boot soldiers wore on the march, so it is what they marched in.

clue.text: US mission after modern scraps of French

indicators.note: scraps means throws away, so the French word is discarded

parts.note: a la mode is French for in the fashion, which means modern, after the fashion
de is French for of

explanation.surface: An American delegation turns up after some bits of French were dropped.
explanation.walkthrough: A LA MODE (in fashion, modern) loses DE, French for 'of', which 'scraps' removes. The Alamo was a Spanish mission in Texas, famous for its 1836 siege.
explanation.definitionFit: The Alamo was a Spanish mission in San Antonio, Texas, later the fort of the famous siege.

clue.text: Did some rapid shooting, perhaps, bagging a rabbit in a tick

indicators.note: in says the first pieces go inside the tick

parts.note: a ked is a sheep tick, a bloodsucking parasite
rabbit, from cockney rhyming slang rabbit and pork, means talk, as does yak

explanation.surface: A gunman shot quickly, bagging a rabbit in seconds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rapid shooting' suggests gunfire, but it is shooting rapids in a canoe-like boat. 'Rabbit' is British slang for chatter; 'bagging' and the second 'a' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: Paddling a small boat down white water is called shooting the rapids, which this verb describes.

clue.text: One Dane involved with Corn Law

indicators.note: involved means tangled up, so these letters are mixed into a new order

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A Danish man is mixed up in the Corn Laws.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Involved' scrambles I DANE CORN; 'with' is a link word. The Corn Laws were 19th-century British tariffs on imported grain.
explanation.definitionFit: An ordinance is an authoritative decree or regulation, a kind of law.

clue.text: Stab heel

definitions.meaning: an attempt, as in to have a go at something
to lean over to one side, as a ship does

explanation.definitionFit: A tilt is an attempt or thrust, as in having a tilt at something; to tilt is to lean, as a heeling ship does.

clue.text: Old country lanes heard cracking up

indicators.note: heard says the word for lanes is spoken, giving a word of the same sound

parts.note: lanes are roads

indicators.note: in a down clue up means reading from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: A1, written AI, means first-rate or cracking

explanation.surface: Roads in an old land are said to be breaking up.
explanation.walkthrough: ROADS said aloud gives RHODES; AI (A1, excellent) turned by 'up' gives IA. Rhodesia was the old name of Zimbabwe.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhodesia is the former name of the country now called Zimbabwe, so it is an old country.

clue.text: Breaking into song, friend grabs Henry in place of Joseph

indicators.note: the friend breaks into the song, so the song's letters are split open around it

parts.note: an aria is a song in an opera

indicators.note: the friend grabs Henry, holding that letter inside itself

parts.note: mate is British slang for a friend
H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance

explanation.surface: A pal bursts into song and seizes someone called Henry, standing in for Joseph.
explanation.walkthrough: Joseph of Arimathea is the man in the Gospels who gave his tomb for the burial of Jesus, so the town is his place.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gospels name Joseph by his home town, calling him Joseph of Arimathea.

clue.text: High notes in range

parts.note: the range is a mountain range, and the high notes are the warbling falsetto calls of an Alpine singer there

explanation.walkthrough: 'Range' looks like a singer's vocal range, but it is a range of mountains, home of the Alpine herdsman's warbling song.
explanation.definitionFit: A yodel is a song switching rapidly to falsetto, traditionally sung in the Alps.

clue.text: Maybe lock toilet before powerful draught becomes progressive

parts.note: in rugby a lock is one of the forwards, so a lock is an example of a forward
loo is British slang for a toilet
in draughts (checkers), a piece that reaches the far side is crowned a king, the most powerful piece

explanation.surface: Someone bolts the bathroom door before a gale blows in, and is somehow called modern-minded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draught' reads as a gust of air, but it is a piece in draughts, the British name for checkers. 'Before' and 'becomes' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone progressive looks ahead to the future, which is what a forward-thinking person does.

clue.text: Ceremony for girl in Youth Club reportedly hands Virginia horse

parts.note: a bat is a club used in sport

indicators.note: reportedly says a word is heard rather than seen, so its sound is used

parts.note: mitts is slang for hands
VA is the US postal abbreviation for Virginia
horse is slang for heroin, abbreviated H

explanation.surface: A girl at a youth club is said to be passing a horse to someone from Virginia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Youth Club' looks like one thing but splits: youth ends the definition and club starts the wordplay. Horse is slang for heroin.
explanation.definitionFit: A bat mitzvah is the Jewish coming-of-age ceremony held for a girl at twelve or thirteen.

clue.text: Daily encountering the unknown makes us cautious

parts.note: a daily, or char, is a British cleaning lady who comes in every day
Y is one of the unknowns in algebra, alongside x and z

explanation.surface: Meeting the mysterious puts us on our guard each day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daily' looks like an adverb or a newspaper; in British usage it is a cleaner, also called a char or charwoman.
explanation.definitionFit: To be chary is to be wary and reluctant to take risks, a synonym of cautious.

clue.text: Cleopatra might have survived had this surfaced

definitions.text: Cleopatra might have survived had this
definitions.meaning: Cleopatra died from the bite of a snake, so she would have lived had the snake stopped in its tracks
covered with a hard road surface made from tarmac

explanation.surface: A whimsical thought about how the Egyptian queen could have lived.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as ASP HALTED: the asp is the snake Cleopatra used to kill herself.
explanation.definitionFit: A road that has been asphalted has been given a hard surface of bitumen mixed with stones.

clue.text: Wild woods in an alpine region

indicators.note: wild here means out of control, so the letters of the following words run loose into a new order

explanation.surface: Untamed forest stands in a mountainous area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild' signals rearranging the letters of WOODS IN AN.
explanation.definitionFit: Snowdonia is the mountainous national park in north Wales around Snowdon, its highest peak.

clue.text: Pick up broadcasts in this area

indicators.note: broadcasts means sent out over the air to be heard, so the phrase is used for its sound

parts.note: over here means in this place, nearby

explanation.surface: A radio receives programmes in the local area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pick up' suggests radio reception; it means catch someone's words by chance. 'Broadcasts' signals a spoken phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: To pick up a remark can mean hearing it unintentionally, which is eavesdropping by accident.

clue.text: After cuts nurses plan a demonstration walk

indicators.note: once the surrounding letters are cut away, what remains is a run hidden inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: Following budget cuts, nursing staff organise a protest march.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After cuts' looks like the news story's setting; it tells you to cut the ends off the following words, leaving the run inside nursES PLAN A DEmonstration.
explanation.definitionFit: An esplanade is a long open promenade, often by the sea, where people walk.

clue.text: Is one also an elder partner in crime?

parts.note: an gives the letter A
in the phrase elders and betters, an elder is a better, a superior

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about whether an older accomplice is something more.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'elders and betters' makes 'an elder' A BETTER. 'Is one also' is the linking frame.
explanation.definitionFit: An abetter encourages or helps someone commit a crime, an accomplice or partner in crime.

clue.text: Old engine driver by son's side

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for son, as in family trees
a side is a team, as in a football side

explanation.surface: A retired train driver stands next to his son.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Engine driver' suggests a train driver, but it is the power that drove old engines. 'By' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Steam power drove old railway locomotives and factory engines, so it is what drove them.

clue.text: Battered crisp coating that is hotter

indicators.note: the shuffled letters coat the other piece, wrapping round it
battered means knocked about, so the word's letters are knocked into a new order

parts.note: IE is the abbreviation for id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: A fried, crunchy batter coating has more kick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Battered' scrambles CRISP into SPICR, which coats IE. The surface suggests food fried in batter.
explanation.definitionFit: Spicier food has more spice, so it tastes hotter on the tongue.

clue.text: With which Head recalls youth to attend?

definitions.text: With which Head recalls youth to attend?

parts.words: With which Head recalls youth to attend?
parts.note: it reads like a headteacher summoning a pupil, but the head is the one on your shoulders, styled to recall a boy attendant at a wedding

explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' looks like a headmaster and 'youth to attend' like a pupil called in; the head wears a style recalling a young attendant.
explanation.definitionFit: This hairstyle is a straight bob with the ends curled under, named after the hair of young servants of old.

clue.text: Poor grain's missing the odd root

indicators.note: the odd-numbered letters are dropped, leaving the second, fourth and so on

explanation.surface: Poor-quality grain lacks the occasional kernel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Missing the odd' removes letters 1, 3, 5... of POOR GRAINS, leaving the even ones.
explanation.definitionFit: Orris is the fragrant root of certain irises, used in perfume.

clue.text: Creature in fur coat, feigning modesty, quietly accepted

parts.note: coy means pretending to be shy or modest
p, piano, is the musical direction for quietly
U means acceptable to the upper class, socially accepted

explanation.surface: A woman in fur pretends to be shy and is quietly let in.
explanation.walkthrough: U is a British label for upper-class, socially accepted usage.
explanation.definitionFit: The coypu is a large South American rodent farmed for its fur, called nutria.

clue.text: One left after having wound up right accounts

indicators.note: in a down clue up means reading from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: ACS is short for accounts

explanation.surface: Someone left wounded has to set the books straight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wound' looks like the past of wind, as in wound up; it is the noun, an injury, and 'up' alone signals the turnaround.
explanation.definitionFit: A scar is the mark that remains on the skin after a wound has healed.

clue.text: Meet standards for downsizing computer department?

definitions.meaning: to be good enough, an idiom for making the grade
a company slimming down might reduce its IT (information technology) team

explanation.surface: A firm meets its targets by trimming the IT office.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the phrase literally: CUT the IT department. 'For' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: To cut it, as in cut the mustard, means to perform well enough to meet the required standard.

clue.text: Vary title on rearranging a certain type of programme

indicators.note: rearranging says the letters of the words before it are put in a different order

explanation.surface: A producer changes a show's name by reshuffling the words.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rearranging' acts on VARY TITLE; 'on' is a link word, and 'Vary' is fodder, not a second signal.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a genre of television show filming real, unscripted people, often in contrived situations.

clue.text: International movement stopping light affliction?

parts.note: a red traffic light tells drivers to stop
a cross is a burden or trouble one has to bear

explanation.surface: A worldwide campaign halts some minor ailment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light affliction' looks like a mild illness; the light is a traffic signal and the affliction a burden to bear.
explanation.definitionFit: The Red Cross is the worldwide humanitarian movement founded in Geneva to aid victims of war and disaster.

clue.text: Bellyache that hurts, by George!

parts.note: GR stands for Georgius Rex, King George, seen on British postboxes
ouch is what you cry out when something hurts

explanation.surface: Someone moans about a pain in the stomach, with an old-fashioned oath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bellyache' is a verb here, to complain, not a stomach pain. 'By' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: To bellyache is informal for to complain, and to grouch means to grumble the same way.
